text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse:
Jonah 1:1 Jonah the prophet had long attempted to rouse the sinful Northern kingdom of Israel to repentance. Sadly, his many sermons and prophecies had fallen on deaf ears. Therefore, YHWH decided to topple Israel, by having them exiled by the up-and-coming Assyrian empire. However, to be worthy of executing this Divine retribution, the Assyrians had to demonstrate their moral superiority to Israel, for they too were sinful. So YHWH sent Jonah to Nineveh to test whether the Assyrians could, at least, be roused to repentance, or whether they too would ignore the prophet’s call. Should they hearken to his words and change their ways, they would have demonstrated their worthiness to become the agents of YHWH.
And so the word of YHWH came to Jonah as follows.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse: Jonah 1:2 “Get up, go to the vast city of Nineveh, and call to it to repent, for their bad behavior has also risen to such proportions before Me that My providence can no longer ignore it.”
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse:
Jonah 1:3 Jonah, who understood that success in this mission would spell disaster for the Israelites, decided to disobey YHWH. For although a prophet is legally required, at pain of death, to share his prophetic messages (Sanhedrin 89a), YHWH had not entrusted him with a specific prophetic message. Rather, He had enlisted him as a preacher.
Concerned that at any moment YHWH would endow him with a specific prophecy that would legally bind him to the mission, Jonah got up to flee from Israel – where prophets could encounter the prophetic presence of YHWH – to Tarshish – where they could not. He dared not travel via the desert, for in the past, prophets with prior prophetic experience in Israel continued to encounter prophecy in the surrounding deserts. Instead, he opted to travel by sea, hoping that the combination of seasickness and idolatrous company would make him immune to prophecy. And so he descended from the highlands to the port of Jaffa and found a ship that had just arrived from Tarshish and was not due to set sail for a number of days. However, upon offering to pay the equivalent fare of a full ship’s cargo, they agreed to set sail immediately. Thus, he boarded the ship to voyage to Tarshish with them, away from the prophetic presence of YHWH. It also morally suited him to rent an entire ship, for fearing adverse consequences at sea, he wished to place as few innocent bystanders as possible in harm’s way.
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse: Jonah 1:4 Indeed, as Jonah surmised, a great storm unfolded at sea, for YHWH cast a great and mighty wind into the sea. That the storm was providential was most apparent, for the storm appeared to emanate from the very ocean surrounding Jonah’s ship – tossing it from side to side, while the surrounding ships continued on their merry ways in tranquil waters. It seemed that the ship – that is, its mast and sails – would be wrecked by the winds, and ultimately sunk by the towering waves.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse: Jonah 1:5 The sailors were terrified and each one cried out to his god hoping to appease the divine wrath. Moreover, they threw the ship’s heavy cargo overboard into the sea, to lighten their load and ride higher in the waters. Jonah, on the other hand, slipped down into the ship’s hold, where he lay down and fell asleep. By lying at the bottom of the ship where the raging waters would first accumulate, he hoped that he would be rapidly drowned, whereupon the storm would cease instantly and spare the lives of the sailors. Moreover, he feared that if he remained on deck, he might be swept up by the waves and cast onto dry land.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse: Jonah 1:6 But he was discovered by the captain who approached him and said to him, “How can you sleep!? Get up and call to Elohim, for perhaps it is your god who is vengeful! We can but hope that maybe the god will revise his plans for us and we will not be obliterated.”
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse: Jonah 1:7 And so they prayed and beseeched the gods, but the storm raged on, unabated. They then said to one another, “Let us proceed to cast lots to identify who has angered the gods and brought this evil upon us, or who possesses insight as to why the gods are angry with us.” They cast many lots to ensure no mistakes, and remarkably each lot fell on Jonah.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse: Jonah 1:8 They then said to him, “Pray tell us if you have sinned, and, if you are innocent, tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. And tell us too of your demographic profile for perhaps you are incompatible with the god of the ocean: What is your profession? From where do you come? What is your country? Who are your people?”
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse: Jonah 1:9 He replied to them, “I am a wayfarer without a fixed home, and I am in the prophetic service of YHWH the God of the heavens of whom I am in perpetual awe. It is thus inconceivable that the god of the ocean should find me distasteful, for it is YHWH who created both the oceans and the dry land.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse: Jonah 1:10 The men were stricken with great awe of YHWH and said to him rebukingly, “What have you done? How dare you attempt to escape YHWH’s calling!”, for the men now knew that he was fleeing the prophetic presence of YHWH, for he had now told them of it.
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse: Jonah 1:11 They then said to him, “What must we do with you to calm the oceans that rage against us, for the sea is becoming increasingly stormy? Shall we steer towards Assyria and Nineveh as YHWH requested of you, or shall we head back to the docks at Jaffa?”
text.0_Chapter, 11_Verse: Jonah 1:12 But he said to them, “You shall not return me to land, lest I be compelled to fulfil my mission. Rather, raise me over the railings and cast me into the sea. Then the sea shall become calm for you. For I know for certain that this great storm has come upon you because of my past misdeed; that this storm is directed at me and not at you.”
text.0_Chapter, 12_Verse: Jonah 1:13 However, the sailor-men were uncertain, for perhaps YHWH now expected them to coerce Jonah into fulfilling his mission. To throw him into the sea could be complicity in his crime. So they attempted to row the ship back to the dry land of Jaffa but were unable to do so, for the sea became ever stormier.
text.0_Chapter, 13_Verse: Jonah 1:14 Upon realizing that YHWH seemed intent on drowning the unremorseful Jonah as punishment for his defiance, they concluded that they had no alternative but to throw him overboard. They called out to YHWH and said, “Please do not hold us accountable for shedding an innocent man’s blood, for this is Your doing YHWH, in accordance with Your will. Surely we need not all perish to avoid actively participating in taking this man’s life.”
text.0_Chapter, 14_Verse: Jonah 1:15 And so they raised Jonah and cast him into the sea, whereupon its raging ceased.1[1] Malbim adds, citing Midrash Tanchuma, that they first experimented with dipping him into the sea. Each time his body contacted the water, the sea calmed; each time they lifted him back up, it raged again. Thus they became confident that YHWH indeed expected them to send him to a watery death. However, Malbim’s suggestion that these details are implied in the text of this pasuk is difficult, since the very terms in question were previously used by Jonah in pasuk 12.
text.0_Chapter, 15_Verse: Jonah 1:16 The sailor-men were greatly awed by YHWH. They offered sacrifices to YHWH and accepted religious oaths upon themselves.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse: Jonah 2:1 YHWH providentially appointed a large male fish2[2] Malbim, pointing to a slight textual clue, adopts the additional narrative of Yalkut Shimoni, according to which Jonah was spewed by the male fish and swallowed whole once more by a female fish whose roe-stuffed abdomen was severely cramped. to swallow Jonah whole. Jonah spent three days and three nights inside the fish’s gut. That he did not suffocate is a natural impossibility, pointing at miraculous intervention. This in-utero-like experience was to symbolize Jonah’s rebirth.
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse: Jonah 2:2 Eventually, Jonah reopened his lines of communication with YHWH. He prayed to his God YHWH from the claustrophobic gut of the female fish.
text.1_Chapter, 2_Verse: Jonah 2:3 He said as follows: “I previously called out to YHWH amidst my distress and He answered me, thus I now beseech You from this abyssal abdomen, for You hearken to my voice.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse: Jonah 2:4 For, when You had me cast into the depths, into the heart of the sea; when I was surrounded by raging torrents of water, when all Your towering waves and crashing surf swept over me –
text.1_Chapter, 4_Verse: Jonah 2:5 I said to myself: I am finished; expelled from the presence of Your providential eye. Yet, following Your miraculous intervention – the arrival of the oxygenated male fish – I realized that I shall continue to prophetically gaze upon Your sanctuary.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse: Jonah 2:6 Then, when the male fish spewed me into the depths of the ocean, the waters encroached on my very life; the depths surrounded me, with seaweed bedecking my head.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse: Jonah 2:7 When I descended beneath the lower extremes of mountains, when the vast land mass shut her bars over me for eternity, once more, YHWH my God, You raised my life from the abyss. You miraculously sent an oxygenated female fish to save me.
text.1_Chapter, 7_Verse: Jonah 2:8 Thus, now, I have penitentially remembered You YHWH, as my life ebbs away in this cramped fish gut. I am certain that my prayer has come before You, that it has reached Your sanctuary.
text.1_Chapter, 8_Verse: Jonah 2:9 I shall go to Nineveh as per Your instructions. I shall fear not lest they repent, for shall those who preserve untrue vanities forsake their despicables – their pagan deities?
text.1_Chapter, 9_Verse: Jonah 2:10 I shall sacrifice a todah sacrifice to You accompanied by the songful voice of gratitude, I shall fulfil my oaths and be faithful to You. And, I shall trust in YHWH’s salvation that I shall cause no harm to befall Israel.”
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse: Jonah 2:11 It was then that YHWH’s providence stirred the mind of the fish, and it spewed Jonah onto the dry land.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse: Jonah 3:1 As he had feared, upon his return to dry land, the word of YHWH came to Jonah a second time, this time with a specific and explicit prophecy, as follows:
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse: Jonah 3:2 Get up, go to the vast city of Nineveh, and proclaim to its inhabitants the message that I now communicate to you. For, because you tarried, they have morally declined to the point that not only are they unworthy of conquering the Israelites, they are even deserving of their own destruction.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse: Jonah 3:3 So Jonah got up and went to Nineveh as per the specific message of YHWH. He intended to deliver YHWH’s specific message regarding their impending destruction, but not to rouse them to repentance as YHWH had originally requested, for he had convinced himself that repentance was beyond them. Now, Nineveh was an enormous city of godly proportions – it took three days to walk from one side to the other.
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse: Jonah 3:4 Upon reaching the outskirts of Nineveh, Jonah progressively entered ever deeper into the city, undertaking a full day’s walk. There, on the second day, he proclaimed and said: “So says YHWH: In a full forty days’ time, Nineveh shall be overturned.” To ensure there would be no miscalculations of the forty days, for the distal neighborhoods of the city would only receive the news almost three days after the proximal ones, he proclaimed the deadline on the second day in the middle of the city, explicitly starting the count only the following day.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse: Jonah 3:5 The people of Nineveh believed the divine words. They proclaimed a fast and donned sackcloth, from their old to their young, hoping to appease Elohim3[3] It is noteworthy that the Assyrians never use the name YHWH in this narrative. Although Malbim doesn’t explicitly say so, perhaps this is textual evidence for Malbim and Abarbanel’s assumption that the inhabitants of Nineveh remained pagan polytheists throughout. through humility and prayer. However, they did not repent, for they presumed themselves innocent, and Jonah had not informed them that YHWH’s decree was the result of their sins.
text.2_Chapter, 5_Verse: Jonah 3:6 However, when word of the decree reached the king of Nineveh, he immediately understood that fasting and mourning were necessary but insufficient, for it was repentance that Elohim sought. He arose from his throne and removed his royal mantle. He donned sackcloth and sat on a bed of ashes.
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse: Jonah 3:7 He issued an urgent edict, and had it communicated throughout Nineveh in the name of the king and his great advisors as follows: “Man and beast, cattle and flock, may not taste a morsel. They may neither graze nor drink water.”
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse: Jonah 3:8 “Man and beast must be covered with sackcloth, and they must call out to Elohim with intensity.” “Finally,” he insisted, “Everyone must repent from their evil ways, and return any loot that they hold in their palms – for one can hardly claim remorse and beg for divine forgiveness before one has taken the available practical steps to set the wrong right. Moreover, to Elohim, financial corruption is the final straw that seals a society’s fate.”
text.2_Chapter, 8_Verse: Jonah 3:9 “If Elohim has sent His prophet to warn us of our impending doom, there must be something we can do about it. Thus, everyone who knows they have sinned shall repent, and the Elohim will change His mind about the decree. He will withdraw from His present state of flaming anger, and we will not be destroyed.”
text.2_Chapter, 9_Verse: Jonah 3:10 The Elohim saw their deeds, that they had taken active measures to repent from their evil ways, by returning stolen goods to their rightful owners. The Elohim changed His mind about the bad decree He told them He would providentially enact against them and did not implement it. Thus, the natural course of history persisted, and Nineveh, in the heartland of the Assyrian empire, continued to thrive.
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse: Jonah 4:1 Remarkably, the inhabitants of Nineveh were spared even though they were still resolutely pagan. Thus Jonah became deeply distressed, for his former assumption – “I shall fear not lest they repent, for shall those who preserve untrue vanities forsake their despicables” – had been most mistaken. It was corruption that had rankled YHWH; not idolatrousness. And now, Jonah’s worst fears had come true. Through his own doing, the Assyrians had repented and been spared, and moreover, had proven themselves worthy of becoming YHWH’s human instrument for punishing Israel. This was most terrible to Jonah, and he was infuriated.
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse: Jonah 4:2 He prayed to YHWH and said, “Please YHWH, did I not already voice my concerns about this very eventuality while still on my home turf, back in Israel!? That is why I preemptively fled to Tarshish. For I knew that Nineveh would be spared if I preached on your behalf, for You are a gracious deity and merciful, slow to anger, overwhelmingly kind, and One who tends to change His mind about enacting bad decrees! Look, they are still resolutely pagan, and yet You spared them!”
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse: Jonah 4:3 “I cannot live in the knowledge that those who will barbarically assault Israel survived because of me. So YHWH, please take my life now, for I will be better off dead than alive.”
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse: Jonah 4:4 But YHWH prophetically said to him in response, “Does it so utterly4[4] I preferred Radak (and Sforno) over Malbim’s interpretation of this pasuk, according to which YHWH challenged Jonah’s concerns of proclaiming false prophecy. Malbim’s interpretation implies that YHWH misunderstood Jonah’s upset. Moreover, the verb charah seems inappropriate if Jonah was distressed rather than angry. Finally, this same phrase appears in pasuk 9, and I preferred a consistent interpretation. infuriate you that others improved themselves because of you?”
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse: Jonah 4:5 Disheartened, Jonah left the city of Nineveh and camped to the east of the city. There, he built a makeshift gazebo for himself, and sat beneath it, in the shady spots it provided. He intended to stay there to observe what would ultimately happen to the city. He hoped that perhaps YHWH’s decree would still be enacted in some partial form, or perhaps their penitential steps would be short-lived5[5] Radak, Sforno. and they would regress to their former evil.
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse: Jonah 4:6 However, his stay proved untenable, for his gazebo provided minimal and patchy shade and the sun continually beat down on his head, causing him great discomfort. Until, one day, YHWH Elohim providentially arranged for a kikayon plant. It climbed above Jonah to provide adequate shade for his head and save him from his unpleasant predicament. Jonah was very pleased with the kikayon, for not only did it improve his physical condition, but surely it was a sign from YHWH that He viewed his camping with favor, for he would indeed be rewarded with witnessing Nineveh’s ultimate downfall.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse: Jonah 4:7 But the very next day, at dawn, the Elohim providentially arranged for a hungry worm, that attacked the roots of the kikayon and caused it to dry out and die.
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse: Jonah 4:8 As the sun rose over the horizon, Elohim providentially arranged for a harsh, ear-splitting easterly wind whose heat, combined with the sun beating on Jonah’s head, caused him to feel faint and collapse6[6] Metzudat Zion, Radak. He begged his soul to depart from his body and let him die, for he said, “I am better off dead than alive.”
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse: Jonah 4:9 Elohim then said to Jonah, “Does the fate of a lowly kikayon utterly infuriate you? Is it worthy of such a reaction?” To which he replied, “Indeed it utterly infuriates me, and for good reason7[7] See pasuk 4 and footnote there. Here too, for consistency, I preferred Radak as the literal interpretation, adding Malbim as an elaborative detail., for its fate has brought me to the verge of death.”
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse: Jonah 4:10 Then YHWH8[8] The continuous changes in God’s names, in this chapter, as well as the end of the previous one, are very puzzling. said, “You have concerned yourself9[9] Malbim suggests that the verb “chas” denotes concern over a third-party’s wellbeing motivated by personal gain. While Malbim proceeds to explain how this applies to Jonah’s dependency on the kikayon, he does not explain how it applies to YHWH’s “dependency” on Nineveh – which is anyway theologically problematic. Thus, I moderated the translation in this context, following Rabbi Eliezer of Beaugency, defining it in the broader sense of “concerning oneself”. with the fate of the kikayon, that you neither labored for nor cultivated, that came to be in a single night and vanished in a single night.”
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse:
Jonah 4:11 “Yet, I should not concern myself with the fate of Nineveh, the massive city! For, although it is pagan, it contains many more than one-hundred-and-twenty-thousand innocent people who were not afforded the education to discern between left – pagan metaphysics rooted in empirical natural phenomena – and right – abstract monotheistic metaphysics, as well as many innocent animals!?” By inference however, this does not extend to the Israelites who were presented with the gift of education and are expected to know better.
Thus ends the book of Jonah, which, from an Israelite perspective, offers neither closure nor comfort. Indeed, and likely much to Jonah’s chagrin, the Assyrians would thereafter march south-west and crush the Israelites, eradicating them – in the national sense – from the face of the earth.
